title: This Fish's Tongue Isn't a Tongue. It's a Living Parasite

scenes.text: Something in this snapper's mouth isn't a tongue.
It's a crustacean under three centimetres long. And it got in through the gills.
As a juvenile it swims in, climbs to the mouth and clamps onto the base of the tongue.
Then it drinks the tongue's blood. Starved, the tongue withers to a stub.
The louse grips the stump and takes over the job. The snapper keeps eating, using the parasite as its tongue.
Described in 1983, it was the first parasite ever found replacing an organ. Look again. That tongue is alive.

description:
The tongue-eating louse, Cymothoa exigua, enters a fish through the gills, feeds on the blood of the tongue until it withers, then attaches to the stump and works as a replacement tongue.
It was first described in snappers from the Gulf of California in 1983, the first documented case of a parasite functionally replacing a host organ; females reach about 29 millimetres. The fish keeps feeding.
Would you still eat the fish?
subject: red snapper fish
first_comment: In 2005 a shopper in London found one inside a supermarket red snapper. Which parasite would you least like to meet?
